# Marin (Stanford CRFM)

Marin runs every experiment as a public GitHub issue with W&B links, which makes it the only lab
whose whole experiment record can be browsed: 446 issues carry the `experiment` label as of this
writing, and the 8B and 32B retrospectives name every phase, restart and discarded cooldown.
Final runs so far: Marin 8B (May 2025), Marin 32B (Oct 2025), Snowball 67B-A2B (2026), and a
535B-A23B hero run in progress. Working notes with sources are in `data/notes/marin.md`.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from src.chapter import *  # noqa
import numpy as np
```

## Marin at a glance

Two figures before the detail. First, the released and evaluated checkpoints over time, scored
on Marin's own 19-task base-model average and on MMLU, with circle area proportional to the
cumulative pretraining compute behind each checkpoint. Post-training compute would be drawn as
a ring around the disk, but the 8B instruct model's SFT used 2.6e20 FLOPs, four ten-thousandths
of the base's 6.1e23, so the ring would be indistinguishable from the disk and is omitted; the
32B has no post-trained release. The 2026 runs are missing from this figure because none has a
published benchmark table yet: Delphi's held-out models (March 2026), Snowball 67B-A2B
(pretraining finished August 2026) and the 535B-A23B hero run (in progress) have public loss
curves, which the next figure uses, but no evaluations.

```{python}
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5

pts = pd.DataFrame([
```

Two released dense models in five months is a short series, and the 32B's 19-task average is
*below* the 8B's despite twice the compute: the 19-task suite saturates on easy tasks and the
32B's gains were on MMLU (+7), MMLU-Pro (+9) and BBH. The discarded Bison cooldown sits two
points under Mantis on the same tokens.

Second, every Marin pretraining run with a public loss curve on one axis, three generations of
recipe: the five-width December 2024 ladder and the 2025 dense runs (the 8B with all its phases
stitched together, the three abandoned Tootsie trials, the 32B) in the hand-tuned Llama-style
recipe; Delphi's three held-out compute-optimal models from March 2026 in the AdamH recipe; and
the 2026 mixture-of-experts runs, Snowball 67B-A2B and the 535B-A23B hero run as far as it has
got. The second chart puts them on cumulative compute (6ND, active parameters for the MoEs),
which is what makes sizes and recipes comparable. The first 20B tokens of each run are cut. The
MoE curves are the Paloma c4_en loss under dropless routing (no capacity-factor token dropping);
the hero run's first segment logged a capacity-dropped evaluation instead, which sits about 0.13
nats higher at the same step and is not drawn.

```{python}
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
cur = losses.marin_pretraining_curves()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
plots.loss_curves(cur, x="tokens", ax=ax, ylabel="Paloma c4_en eval loss (nats/token)", min_tokens=2e10,
                  title="Every Marin pretraining run, by cumulative tokens")
ax.set_ylim(2.08, 3.45)   # the 32B's first eval points are above 4 and would set the scale
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
plots.loss_curves(cur, x="flops", ax=ax, ylabel="Paloma c4_en eval loss (nats/token)", min_tokens=2e10,
                  title="Every Marin pretraining run, by cumulative compute (6ND; active parameters for MoEs)")
ax.set_ylim(2.08, 3.45)
plt.show()
```

Three readings from the compute axis.

**Size, within one recipe.** Where the 13B trial stopped (1.8e23 FLOPs) it was at 2.50 against
the 8B's 2.60 at the same compute; the 24B at 3.5e23 was 2.45 against 2.51. The 70B stopped at
6.5e23, just past the finished 8B's 6.1e23, at 2.42 against the 8B's final 2.35: on matched
compute the smaller model won, because it had a cooldown and the 70B never did. That is the same
lesson as the trajectory figure below, from the other side: without a cooldown a trial's loss
understates the model. The ladder's small models, trained to 90 to 900 tokens per parameter, sit
well above everything else at equal compute, which is what over-training past the
compute-optimal point costs.

**Recipe, at equal compute.** Delphi's 1e23 model reached 2.34 on 9.4e22 FLOPs. The 32B, on the
2025 recipe, was at 2.42 when it had spent the same compute, and the 8B at 2.55; the finished
32B needed 1.2e24, thirteen times as much, to get to 2.20. Delphi's 1e22 model likewise beats
the 8B at matched compute by 0.12. Some of that is compute-optimal allocation rather than
recipe, since the 2025 runs were far past optimal tokens per parameter at any given point, but
it is the cleanest cross-generation comparison Marin's record allows.

**Architecture.** Snowball, at 1.2e23 FLOPs of active-parameter compute, ended at 2.27, below
Delphi's 25B dense model at similar compute and below where the 32B was at that compute by
0.12. The hero run at 4.6T tokens (6.3e23 FLOPs so far) is at 2.29, level with where the 32B
was at the same compute, and still at full learning rate with three quarters of its tokens to
go. The 6ND-on-active-parameters convention flatters MoEs, since it ignores the memory and
communication cost of the inactive experts, and the two MoE curves should be read against each
other and against the Marin MoE law rather than as a like-for-like efficiency gain.

Bookkeeping: the 13B trial's curve starts at 1.7T tokens because only its longest restart
segment was fetched; the trials' token axes use the average tokens per step from W&B, since
their batch ramps are not public; Snowball's active parameter count (about 2B) is from the model
name, not a stated figure.

## Returns to post-training compute

Marin has published no RL curve, and its only released post-trained model is the SFT-only 8B
instruct. But one 2026 experiment (issue 3956, April to May 2026) is exactly a returns-to-SFT
sweep: the Marin 8B base fine-tuned on OpenThoughts-4 math subsets of 256, 512, 1,024, 2k, 5k,
10k and 50k examples, each with reasoning traces written by one of eight teacher models, three
training repeats per cell; the 32B base on 10k and 50k with four teachers. Every fine-tune was
scored with evalchemy on AIME 24 and 25, AMC23, HMMT and MATH500, averaged over 3 to 10 sampling
seeds, and the results are public W&B runs. `data/posttraining/marin_sft_scaling.csv` holds the
1,014 averaged evaluations; `src/fetch_evalchemy.py` rebuilds it. SFT compute is not logged, so
the x-axis is 6ND at an assumed 10,000 tokens per example (OpenThoughts traces run to the 32k
cap); the assumption shifts every point by the same factor.

```{python}
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.5
sft = pd.read_csv(load.DATA / "posttraining" / "marin_sft_scaling.csv")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.5))
plots.sft_scaling(sft, "AIME24", ax=axes[0])
plots.sft_scaling(sft, "MATH500", ax=axes[1])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Four readings.

**The shape depends on the benchmark.** MATH500 rises close to log-linearly in SFT compute, from
13 to 28 percent at 256 examples to 66 to 83 percent at 50k on the 8B, roughly seven points per
doubling of data. AIME24 is flat within noise, under 4 percent, through 10k examples and then
jumps to 18 to 36 percent at 50k. A competition benchmark reads as a threshold; a broad one reads
as a smooth return.

**The base model carries through.** At the same data and teacher, the 32B lands 10 to 20 AIME24
points above the 8B (47 against 36 percent with Qwen3-30B-A3B traces at 50k). Pretraining
compute and post-training compute are not substitutes here; the larger base gets more from
every example.

**The teacher matters as much as the data.** At 50k examples on the 8B, traces from
Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking give 36 percent on AIME24 and traces from Qwen3-4B give 18, at identical
SFT compute. What is being bought is distilled capability from a stronger model, so this is a
return to distillation, not to post-training compute alone, and it cannot be read across to RL.

**The compute is tiny.** The 50k-example run is about 2.4e19 FLOPs for the 8B under the stated
assumption, four hundred-thousandths of the 6.1e23 pretraining run; the whole sweep, some 130
fine-tunes, is under 1e21. Whatever the right functional form, the marginal return per FLOP in
this regime is orders of magnitude above the pretraining curve's, which is the standard argument
for why labs moved spend into post-training. Marin's own move is the Snowball post-training
pipeline, which had no published numbers as of September 2026.

## Compute and cost

Marin has never published a dollar figure, a GPU-hour total or a budget. What exists: the compute
was donated (Google's TPU Research Cloud for the 2024 and 2025 runs and for Delphi; the Jen-Hsun
and Lori Huang Foundation's CoreWeave GB200 allocation for the 535B run, out of a total
foundation purchase of about $108M of CoreWeave compute for AI research that is not broken down
by project), development funding came from the Siegel Family Endowment and Schmidt Sciences, and
the team grew from one to about ten FTE between 2025 and 2026. The table converts the 6ND
compute of every sized Marin run into the book's common yardstick, H100-hours at 40 percent
utilisation and $2 per hour; these are what the runs *would* have cost at cloud list price on
GPUs, not what Marin paid, which was nothing in cash for the accelerators.

```{python}
dm = load.runs("marin")
dm = dm[~dm["run_id"].str.contains("aggregate")].copy()
cost = (dm.dropna(subset=["flops"]).groupby(["project", "run_type"], observed=True)["flops"].sum().reset_index())
cost["H100-hours (40% MFU)"] = cost["flops"] / plots.FLOPS_PER_GPU_HOUR
cost["USD at $2/H100-h"] = cost["H100-hours (40% MFU)"] * plots.USD_PER_GPU_HOUR
tot = cost[["flops", "H100-hours (40% MFU)", "USD at $2/H100-h"]].sum()
t = cost.copy(); t["flops"] = t["flops"].map(fmt_flops)
t["H100-hours (40% MFU)"] = t["H100-hours (40% MFU)"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}"); t["USD at $2/H100-h"] = t["USD at $2/H100-h"].map(lambda v: f"${v / 1e6:,.2f}M")
display(t.sort_values(["project", "run_type"]))
display(Markdown(f"All sized Marin runs together: **{tot['flops']:.1e} FLOPs**, about **{tot['H100-hours (40% MFU)'] / 1e6:.1f}M H100-hours** or "
                 f"**${tot['USD at $2/H100-h'] / 1e6:,.0f}M** at list price; the 535B hero run alone is {2.7e24 / tot['flops']:.0%} of it. "
                 "Rows typed `final` include the released 8B and 32B and the Snowball and 535B runs; `aborted` is the discarded 32B cooldown, "
                 "rescues and the 13B/24B/70B trials; `ladder` is Delphi, the MoE sweeps and the 2024 width ladder."))
```

The share that did not ship (aborted plus ladder plus ablation rows) is the experiment share
this book is after, and for Marin it is a floor: the 446-issue long tail of small ablations has
no compute attached, and the 2026 MoE screening cells (about 80 runs at d512 to d1280) are one row.
People are the other missing half. At ten FTE and a fully loaded US research-engineer cost of
$300k to $500k a year, Marin's labour bill is a few million dollars a year, the same order as the
list-price value of a year of its compute; but neither number is Marin's, and the lab has not
published either.

## Algorithmic efficiency across recipe generations

The cleanest measure of algorithmic progress a lab's own record allows is the compute its
*finished* runs needed to reach a given loss, generation by generation. Finished matters: under a
warmup-stable-decay schedule the loss drops at the cooldown wherever it happens to fall, so the
point along a curve where it first crosses a threshold mostly measures where the cooldown was,
not how good the recipe is. The figure below therefore uses only endpoints: the five December
2024 ladder runs, the two 2025 dense releases, Delphi's three 2026 held-out models, and Snowball.
The 13B, 24B and 70B trials and the running hero are excluded because they never cooled down. A
power law is drawn through each generation's endpoints; dashed where extrapolated.

```{python}
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
curd = {c.name: c for c in cur}
end = lambda n: (float(curd[n].flops[-1]), float(curd[n].loss[-1]))
gen_rows = []
for n in [k for k in curd if k.startswith("ladder")]:
    gen_rows.append(("Dec 2024 width ladder (210B tokens each)", n.replace("ladder ", ""), *end(n), "dense"))
for n in ["Marin 8B (Tootsie)", "Marin 32B (Mantis)"]:
    gen_rows.append(("2025 dense recipe (Llama-style, hand-tuned)", n.split(" (")[0], *end(n), "dense"))
for n in ["Delphi 1e21 (3.4B)", "Delphi 1e22 (9.7B)", "Delphi 1e23 (25B)"]:
    gen_rows.append(("Mar 2026 Delphi (AdamH, compute-optimal)", n, *end(n), "dense"))
gen_rows.append(("2026 MoE (Snowball 67B-A2B)", "Snowball", *end("Snowball 67B-A2B"), "moe"))
gen = pd.DataFrame(gen_rows, columns=["generation", "name", "flops", "loss", "kind"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
_, gfits = plots.generation_frontier(gen, ax=ax, guides=[2.35, 2.27], ylabel="Final Paloma c4_en eval loss (nats/token)",
                                     title="Finished Marin runs by recipe generation: final loss against total compute")
plt.show()
f25, fD = gfits["2025 dense recipe (Llama-style, hand-tuned)"], gfits["Mar 2026 Delphi (AdamH, compute-optimal)"]
inv = lambda f, L: (f.A / L) ** (1 / f.alpha)
snow = end("Snowball 67B-A2B")
display(Markdown(f"At c4_en **2.35** (the finished 8B's loss): 2025 recipe {inv(f25, 2.35):.1e} FLOPs, Delphi {inv(fD, 2.35):.1e}, "
                 f"a **{inv(f25, 2.35) / inv(fD, 2.35):.1f}x** reduction in about ten months. At Snowball's **{snow[1]:.3f}**: the 2025 line needs "
                 f"{inv(f25, snow[1]):.1e}, Delphi's line (extrapolated {inv(fD, snow[1]) / 9.4e22:.1f}x past its largest run) {inv(fD, snow[1]):.1e}, "
                 f"Snowball used {snow[0]:.1e}: **{inv(f25, snow[1]) / snow[0]:.1f}x** over 2025 and **{inv(fD, snow[1]) / snow[0]:.1f}x** over Delphi, "
                 "on active-parameter compute."))
```

Three cautions on reading this as a rate of algorithmic progress. The generations differ in data
as well as recipe (DCLM and Nemotron-CC for the 2025 runs, a Nemotron, StarCoder and ProofPile
mix for Delphi), and c4_en is a web-text loss, so part of the gap is data mix. The 2025 runs
were trained far past compute-optimal tokens per parameter, so part of the gap is allocation
rather than optimizer or architecture; Delphi's own contribution was to make the allocation
principled. And MoE compute on active parameters ignores the memory and communication cost of
the inactive experts, which is why Marin quotes its MoE gain as 6.7x theoretical but 3.6x
realised on TPU v4. Marin's own stated multipliers, on its Paloma macro-loss metric, are: the May
2026 recipe law against the April MoE law, which at equal loss implies about 2.1x less compute
in seven weeks (the coefficient fell from 95.18 to 88.90 at a shared exponent of 0.0941); the MoE
recipe against Delphi, 3.6x realised; and the 2025 optimizer benchmark, at most 1.4x over AdamW
at 130M shrinking to about 1.1x at 1.2B. Taken together with the endpoint frontier, Marin's
record is consistent with something like a 5 to 10x fall in compute-to-loss between the 2025
and 2026 recipes, most of it from compute-optimal allocation and the AdamH recipe, with MoE
adding a further two-fold on the active-parameter accounting.

## All scaling experiments over time

Every Marin experiment with a date, on one time axis. The six families that produced a scaling
curve are drawn as insets on shared axes (compute 1e17 to 1e25 FLOPs on x, loss 2.0 to 3.8 on y),
each above its date, so their shapes and ranges can be compared directly; every other dated
experiment in `experiments.csv` is a tick on the timeline, coloured by stage. The insets do not
share a metric: the ladder and Tootsie panels are Paloma c4_en, Delphi is its Nemotron-mix eval
loss, and the two MoE laws are Paloma macro loss, so compare shapes across panels, not levels.

```{python}
#| column: page
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7.5
delphi = pd.read_csv(load.DATA / "experiments_data" / "marin_delphi_ladder.csv")

def draw_ladder(ax):
    lad = [c for n, c in curd.items() if n.startswith("ladder")]
    x = np.array([c.flops[-1] for c in lad]); y = np.array([c.loss[-1] for c in lad])
    f = fits.fit_power_law(x, y); xs = np.geomspace(x.min(), 3e24, 50)
    ax.plot(xs, f.predict(xs), color=plots.MUTED, lw=1, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=18, c=plots.RUN_COLORS["ladder"], zorder=3)

def draw_tootsie(ax):
    for c, kind in [(curd["Marin 8B (Tootsie)"], "final"), (curd["Marin 32B (Mantis)"], "final"),
                    (curd["13B trial"], "aborted"), (curd["24B trial"], "aborted"), (curd["70B trial"], "aborted")]:
        k = c.tokens >= 2e10; col = plots.RUN_COLORS["final"] if kind == "final" else plots.MUTED
        ax.plot(c.flops[k], c.loss[k], color=col, lw=1 if kind == "final" else 0.8, ls="-" if kind == "final" else (0, (2, 2)))
        ax.scatter([c.flops[-1]], [c.loss[-1]], s=40 if kind == "final" else 14, marker="*" if kind == "final" else "x", c=col, zorder=3)

def draw_delphi(ax):
    iso = delphi[delphi["kind"] == "isoflop"]; opt = delphi[delphi["kind"] == "optimum"]
    ho = delphi[(delphi["kind"] == "held_out") & (delphi["seed"] == "default")]
    ax.scatter(iso["total_gflops"] * 1e9, iso["loss"], s=8, c=plots.MUTED, alpha=0.6, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(opt["C_flops"], opt["loss_star"], color=plots.RUN_COLORS["ladder"], lw=1.2, zorder=3)
    f = fits.fit_power_law(opt["C_flops"], opt["loss_star"], irreducible=True); xs = np.geomspace(3e20, 3e23, 50)
    ax.plot(xs, f.predict(xs), color=plots.RUN_COLORS["ladder"], lw=1, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
    ax.scatter(ho["C_nom"], ho["loss"], s=40, marker="*", c=plots.RUN_COLORS["final"], zorder=4)

def draw_moe_law(ax, A, lo, hi, val=None):
    law = fits.stated_fit(E=1.6, A=A, alpha=0.0941); xs = np.geomspace(1e17, 1e25, 100); inside = (xs >= lo) & (xs <= hi)
    ax.plot(xs[inside], law.predict(xs[inside]), color=plots.RUN_COLORS["ablation"], lw=1.4)
    ax.plot(xs, law.predict(xs), color=plots.RUN_COLORS["ablation"], lw=0.8, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
    if val:
        ax.scatter([val[0]], [val[1]], s=40, marker="*", c=plots.RUN_COLORS["final"], zorder=4)

def draw_hero_ladder(ax):
    for C in [1.8e19, 1.3e20, 9.2e20, 6.7e21]:
        ax.axvline(C, color=plots.RUN_COLORS["ladder"], lw=1)
    ax.axvline(2.7e24, color=plots.RUN_COLORS["final"], lw=1.5, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
    ax.text(0.5, 0.5, "rung sizes only;\nlosses not public", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", fontsize=6.5, color=plots.MUTED)

fams = [
    dict(date="2024-12-16", title="Width ladder (5 runs)", metric="c4_en loss", draw=draw_ladder),
    dict(date="2025-04-01", title="Tootsie 8B / 32B and trials", metric="c4_en loss", draw=draw_tootsie),
    dict(date="2026-03-15", title="Delphi IsoFLOP (81) + held-out", metric="Nemotron-mix eval loss", draw=draw_delphi),
    dict(date="2026-04-06", title="MoE v16 law (fit 1e18 to 1e20)", metric="Paloma macro loss", draw=lambda ax: draw_moe_law(ax, 95.18, 1e18, 1e20, (1e21, 2.599))),
    dict(date="2026-05-30", title="May recipe law (fit 1e18 to 3e19)", metric="Paloma macro loss", draw=lambda ax: draw_moe_law(ax, 88.90, 1e18, 3e19)),
    dict(date="2026-08-15", title="535B hero-shape ladder (4 rungs)", metric="(no losses)", draw=draw_hero_ladder),
]
ex = load.experiments("marin")
def first_date(s):
    s = str(s).strip().split(" to ")[0]
    return pd.Timestamp(s + ("-07-01" if len(s) == 4 else "-15" if len(s) == 7 else ""))
ticks = pd.DataFrame({"date": ex["date"].map(first_date), "label": ex["intervention"].str.slice(0, 38), "stage": ex["stage"]})
fig = plots.experiment_timeline(fams, ticks, xlim=(1e17, 1e25), ylim=(2.0, 3.8),
                                title="Marin's scaling experiments, Nov 2024 to Sep 2026 (insets on shared axes; metric per panel)")
plt.show()
```

The picture is of a lab that ran one width ladder, then trained by hand for a year, then built
the apparatus: within five months of March 2026 it had an IsoFLOP suite validated at 300x, two
successive MoE laws on the same functional form, a learning-rate law, and a hero-shape ladder.
The 2025 panel is the only one whose curves are actual training trajectories rather than fitted
laws or ladder endpoints; everything before it is five points and everything after it is a
formula plus a validation star.

## What is unusual here

Marin's flagship 2025 runs were **not** preceded by a scaling ladder. The 8B was chosen "mostly
out of pragmatism" (reserved capacity) and started "with what we had"; the 32B was "largely a
scale-up of the 8B recipe" and needed two rescues and a discarded cooldown. In 2026 the lab
built the machinery it had lacked: Delphi (an 81-run IsoFLOP suite whose pre-registered forecast
hit the 1e23 run within 0.2 percent at a 300x extrapolation), a mixture-of-experts law validated
at 1e21, a learning-rate law that removed per-size sweeps, and a four-rung ladder costing about
1 percent of the 535B run. So this chapter shows both regimes in one lab: scale-up by hand, then
scale-up by law.

## Compute that did not ship

Where OLMo's development share comes from an accounting paper, Marin's is visible run by run.
The 32B programme discarded a full 1.07T-token cooldown (about 2.1e23 FLOPs) after GSM8K
contamination and a data-permutation artefact were traced, and abandoned an optimizer-state
rebuild and a Muon swap. Three larger Tootsie runs (13B, 24B, 70B) were opened and closed with
empty results. The bar below counts only runs with a size attached, so the 446-issue long tail of
small ablations is missing from it; it is a floor.

```{python}
df = load.runs("marin")
df = df[~df["run_id"].str.contains("aggregate")].copy()   # phase rows already sum to the aggregates
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1.8)); plots.compute_split(df, ax=ax, title="Marin: logged 6ND FLOPs by run type (aggregates removed)"); plt.show()
display(Markdown(f"Non-final share of logged FLOPs: **{load.experiment_share(df):.0%}**; aborted alone: "
                 f"**{df.loc[df['run_type']=='aborted','flops'].sum()/df['flops'].sum():.0%}**."))
```

## The final runs as trajectories

`runs.csv` gives each phase of the 8B and 32B runs its own tokens and FLOPs. That is right for
the compute split and wrong for the loss: the loss at the end of Phoenix reflects every token
since step 0, not the 6.3T on that row. The figure below puts the W&B curves on the honest axis,
cumulative training tokens (the trainer's global step times the batch schedule, which reproduces
the model card's phase totals to within 0.03T), and draws each phase, cooldown and abandoned side
branch as one piece of one trajectory. The metric is the Paloma c4_en eval loss throughout;
train loss moves with the data mix and is not comparable across phases. The first 0.3T tokens
are cut so the warm-up does not set the scale.

```{python}
s8, s32 = losses.marin_8b(), losses.marin_32b()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 9))
plots.loss_trajectory(s8, ax=axes[0], title="Marin 8B: c4_en eval loss over 12.7T tokens",
                      ylabel="Paloma c4_en eval loss (nats/token)", min_tokens=3e11)
plots.loss_trajectory(s32, ax=axes[1], title="Marin 32B: c4_en eval loss over 6.4T tokens",
                      ylabel="Paloma c4_en eval loss (nats/token)", min_tokens=2e11)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
display(Markdown("Start and end of every drawn segment (start = first eval point after the cut):"))
display(pd.concat([losses.phase_table(s8, 3e11), losses.phase_table(s32, 2e11)], ignore_index=True).round(3))
```

Four things are visible here that no per-row number shows.

**Stable phases are nearly flat on this metric.** Kestrel's constant-learning-rate stretch from
2T to 2.77T moved the loss by under 0.01. Phoenix spent 5.5T tokens, 43 percent of the whole
run, between 2.52 and 2.50. Phase 3 of the 32B bought 0.02 over 3T tokens. Under a
warmup-stable-decay schedule the stable phase is banking capability that only shows up in the
decay, so most of the tokens in both runs look wasted on a loss-versus-tokens plot and are not.

**The cooldowns do the visible work.** Starling, the second 8B cooldown, is 1.3T tokens or 10
percent of the run, and took the loss from 2.49 to 2.35: a larger drop than the entire 9T
between 2T and 11T (0.06). The 32B's Mantis cooldown bought 0.07 in 1.07T tokens against
phase 3's 0.02 in 3T. A final-run loss is therefore as much a measurement of cooldown depth as
of scale, which matters when the cross-lab chapter compares final losses across labs.

**The first cooldown bought nothing on c4_en.** Jellyfish ended at 2.605, above the 2.585 where
Ocelot started, while its benchmark gains were real (MMLU 65.3, the reason it was kept). The
70/30 high-quality mix moves the model away from web text, and c4_en is web text. The three
short cooldown branches off Jellyfish (dessert, Raccoon, Spoonbill) all land within 0.02 of it.
Their value was diagnostic: Raccoon and Spoonbill isolated the `lm_head` norm explosion that
led to z-loss in Starling.

**Restarts and rescues leave marks.** Every phase boundary shows a transient: the batch and
learning-rate change into Ocelot, the rewarm into Phoenix, a spike at 5.4T. The 32B's phase 1
spikes are visible even in the sparse eval curve, and its two rescue attempts sit on top of the
trunk and go nowhere (the Muon swap ends 0.045 above where it began). Bison and Mantis ran the
same 1.07T tokens; Mantis sits 0.02 below Bison at matched tokens, so the permutation fix and
MegaMath moved the loss, not only the contaminated GSM8K score.

The trajectory also corrects a comparison made in earlier drafts of this chapter, which read the
abandoned 13B, 24B and 70B trials' final losses against the finished 8B's 2.35. Those trials
never had a cooldown, so that reading is unfair to them. At matched tokens, with no cooldown on
either side, the size advantage was real and grew with size:

```{python}
dm = load.runs("marin")
trials = dm[dm["run_id"].isin(["exp860 Tootsie 13B", "exp861 Tootsie 24B", "exp750 Tootsie 70B"])].copy()
trials["8B trunk loss at same tokens"] = losses.loss_at(s8, trials["tokens"])
trials["gap"] = trials["loss"] - trials["8B trunk loss at same tokens"]
trials["tokens_T"] = trials["tokens"] / 1e12
trials["params"] = trials["params_total"].map(lambda p: f"{p / 1e9:.0f}B")
display(trials[["run_id", "params", "tokens_T", "loss", "8B trunk loss at same tokens", "gap"]].round(3))
```

What Marin gave up in April 2025 was that gap; the losses on the rows understate it.

## The mixture-of-experts law and its held-out point

Marin fitted `loss = 1.6 + 95.18 · C^-0.0941` on a 1e18 to 1e20 IsoFLOP sweep and then trained a
1e21 test: predicted 2.606, measured 2.599. That is the experiments-predict-the-final-run test in
miniature, and the residual is the number the cross-lab chapter wants.

```{python}
law = fits.stated_fit(E=1.6, A=95.18, alpha=0.0941)
xs = np.geomspace(1e18, 3e23, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(xs[xs <= 1e20], law.predict(xs[xs <= 1e20]), color=plots.INK2, lw=2, label="Fit range (1e18 to 1e20)")
ax.plot(xs[xs >= 1e20], law.predict(xs[xs >= 1e20]), color=plots.INK2, lw=2, ls=(0, (4, 3)), label="Extrapolation")
ax.scatter([1e21], [2.599], s=220, marker="*", c=plots.RUN_COLORS["final"], edgecolors=plots.SURFACE, linewidths=2, zorder=4, label="1e21 test run (measured 2.599)")
ax.annotate("predicted 2.606", (1e21, 2.606), xytext=(10, 10), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9, color=plots.INK2)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Training compute (FLOPs)"); ax.set_ylabel("Loss")
ax.set_title("Marin MoE law: 1e18 to 1e20 sweep extrapolated to a 1e21 test"); ax.legend(loc="upper right"); plt.show()
display(Markdown(f"Log residual at 1e21: **{np.log(2.599/2.606):+.4f}**. Elasticity of loss to compute at 1e21 from the law: "
                 f"**{law.elasticity(1e21):.3f}**; at the 2.7e24 hero-run scale it falls to **{law.elasticity(2.7e24):.3f}** "
                 "because the pinned irreducible term dominates."))
```

## Run sizes, compute split, timeline

Losses come from the public `marin-community/marin` W&B project (`data/losses/marin/`; the
metric is the Paloma c4_en eval loss, the one the retrospectives plot, in nats per token with
the Llama 3 tokenizer). Eighteen runs are covered: every 8B phase and cooldown, the 13B, 24B and
70B trials, and the 32B phases, rescues and cooldowns. The standard panel below draws them
without a fitted law, for the reason the trajectory figure makes visible: most rows with a loss
are continuation phases whose `flops` is that phase's compute, not the cumulative compute the
loss reflects, and the cooldown losses are on a different learning-rate footing from the
pretraining phases. Read the abandoned trials against the 8B at matched tokens (table above),
not against the finished stars. Delphi's 81-run grid is one row here; its per-run sizes are in
the repository's hard-coded suite and can be expanded later.

One clean experiment series does exist: a five-width ladder from December 2024
(`tootsie-scaling-*`, hidden 512 to 2048 at 16 layers, each 210B tokens of DCLM-baseline, so 90
to 900 tokens per parameter rather than compute-optimal). Fitting a two-parameter power law to
those five points and extrapolating to the released 8B and 32B is the report's basic move, shown
here on Marin's own data; the residuals are in the table.

```{python}
dm = load.runs("marin")
lad = dm[dm["run_id"].str.startswith("tootsie-scaling-")].dropna(subset=["flops", "loss"]).sort_values("flops")
fin = dm[dm["run_id"].isin(["marin-8b-base-deeper-starling (exp600_tootsie, aggregate)",
                            "marin-32b-base Mantis (aggregate final artifact)"])].dropna(subset=["flops", "loss"])
fit_m = fits.fit_power_law(lad["flops"], lad["loss"]) if len(lad) >= 2 else None
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.scatter(lad["flops"], lad["loss"], s=60, c=plots.PROJECT_SLOTS[0], edgecolors=plots.SURFACE, linewidths=1.5, label="Dec 2024 ladder (210B tokens each)", zorder=3)
ax.scatter(fin["flops"], fin["loss"], s=240, marker="*", c=plots.PROJECT_SLOTS[1], edgecolors=plots.SURFACE, linewidths=2, label="released 8B and 32B", zorder=4)
if fit_m is not None:
    xs = np.geomspace(lad["flops"].min(), fin["flops"].max() * 1.5, 100)
    ax.plot(xs, fit_m.predict(xs), color=plots.MUTED, lw=2, ls=(0, (1, 2)), label=fit_m.label(), zorder=1)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Training compute (FLOPs, 6ND)"); ax.set_ylabel("Paloma c4_en eval loss (nats/token)")
ax.set_title("Marin: ladder law vs released models"); ax.legend(loc="upper right"); plt.show()
if fit_m is not None and not fin.empty:
    t = fin[["run_id", "flops", "loss"]].copy()
    t["predicted"] = fit_m.predict(t["flops"]); t["log_residual"] = np.log(t["loss"]) - np.log(t["predicted"])
    display(t.round(4))
```

The ladder is not a compute-optimal sweep, the law has no irreducible term (so it keeps falling
where a real curve flattens), and the finals sit at the end of long cooldowns on a different data
mix, so the residual mixes all three effects; a 200x to 400x extrapolation from five points is
a demonstration of the method, not a test of Marin's forecasting. It is still the only Marin
curve that runs from experiments to finals on one metric.


## Narrative

**8B "Tootsie".** Llama-3.1-8B shape, 12.7T tokens, on two TPU v5e-256 slices and then a
reserved v4-2048. Phases were named after the fact: Kestrel, Ocelot, Jellyfish (first cooldown),
Phoenix (rewarm and data switch), Starling and Deeper Starling (second cooldown). Side runs that
fed decisions: microanneals that settled the cooldown mix at 70/15/15, "dessert" patch runs, and
two alternative cooldowns. Final 19-task average 66.6 against Llama 3.1 8B's 65.3.

**32B "Mantis".** Phase 1 (Llama-3-style, 80k steps) had persistent loss spikes that clipping
softened but did not fix. Two rescues failed and were discarded. Phase 3 warm-started a Qwen3-32B
backbone with QK-Norm from the 80k weights and the spikes disappeared. The first cooldown was
discarded and rerun on the same tokens after the contamination and permutation bugs were found.

**Scale-up by law (2026).** Delphi, the MoE IsoFLOP law, the MuonH learning-rate law (R² 0.996 on
a 150-run sweep), and the 535B ladder. Marin's recipe document now codifies the sequence: tune at
about 130M and 2.5B tokens, define scaling rules, run an IsoFLOP sweep, run a ladder, promote to a
daily canary. Ideas for the MoE are screened at d512 to d1280 against the fitted law, with
"effective speedup" computed by inverting the law and multiplying by measured throughput.

**Not reconstructable from here.** Delphi's fitted exponent and the 535B
ladder forecast (both in blocked pages or reports), the compute of the long tail of small
ablations, any dollar figure (compute was donated by Google TRC and the Huang Foundation), and
the reasons the 13B, 24B and 70B trials were abandoned (their W&B runs simply stop in April 2025 at 2.3T, 2.4T and 1.5T tokens).
